w: Islamic tradition traces a small prayer hall here to the caliph Umar in the 7th century; the mosque standing today was raised by the Umayyads on the same axis as the Dome of the Rock nearby. Earthquakes flattened it twice, in 746 and 1033, and each time it was rebuilt.
s: Rebuilt after earthquakes, still standing at seven aisles
_facts: Main congregational mosque in the Al-Aqsa compound, Old City of Jerusalem
Tradition holds a small prayer hall was built here by the caliph Umar
Destroyed by earthquakes in 746 and 1033, rebuilt each time
Present structure reduced to seven aisles under the Fatimid caliph al-Zahir

w: The prayer section is a sliver of a much longer retaining wall, 488 metres end to end, built to shore up the hill known as the Temple Mount. The lowest courses date to the close of the Second Temple period, credited to Herod the Great; Umayyad and Ottoman builders added the rest on top.
s: Herod's foundation stones, still standing two millennia on
_facts: Ancient retaining wall of the Temple Mount, 488 metres long overall
Lower courses date from the end of the Second Temple period, begun under Herod the Great
Middle courses added during the Umayyad period, uppermost courses more recent, from the Ottoman period

w: Constantine's builders raised the first church here in the 4th century over the traditional sites of the crucifixion and the empty tomb; al-Hakim tore it down in 1009, rebuilt by 1048. Today it is shared by the Armenian, Greek Orthodox and Latin patriarchates, the tomb sealed inside a 19th-century shrine.
s: Three patriarchates share one roof over Calvary and the tomb
_facts: Fourth-century church in the Christian Quarter of the Old City
Considered the holiest site in Christianity, a pilgrimage site since the 4th century
Destroyed in 1009 by al-Hakim, rebuilt by 1048, modified after the 1099 Crusader capture
The tomb is enclosed by a 19th-century shrine called the Aedicule

w: Built in 691-692 CE for the caliph Abd al-Malik, this octagonal shrine is the oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture, carrying the religion's earliest inscriptions naming the Prophet. It encloses the rock tradition names as the start of the Night Journey - and, for Jews and Christians, Abraham's sacrifice.
s: The oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture
_facts: Built 691-692 CE on the orders of the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik
Oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture
Contains the earliest inscriptions proclaiming Islam and the Prophet Muhammad
Tradition holds the Night Journey of Muhammad began from the rock at its centre; also venerated in Judaism and Christianity as the site of Abraham's sacrifice

w: A single flat-topped hill carries two of history's vanished Temples beneath its plaza, and the standing al-Aqsa Mosque and Dome of the Rock above it - venerated across Judaism, Christianity and Islam alike. Herod's retaining walls, including the Western Wall, still hold the platform up; eleven gates lead in.
s: One hilltop, eleven gates, three faiths' holiest ground
_facts: Hill in the Old City, site of two successive Temples
Home to the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock
Retaining walls, including the Western Wall, originally built by Herod the Great
Reached through eleven gates, ringed by Mamluk-era porticos and four minarets

w: In July 1946, Irgun operatives disguised as workmen and hotel waiters carried a bomb into the basement of the King David Hotel, whose wing housed the British Mandate's civil secretariat and military headquarters. The blast collapsed the wing, killing 91 - the deadliest attack on the British of the Mandate era.
s: A hotel bombing that killed 91, deadliest of the Mandate era
_facts: British administrative and military headquarters were housed in the hotel's southern wing
Bombed on 22 July 1946 by the Irgun during the Jewish insurgency
91 people killed and 46 injured, the deadliest attack on the British during the Mandate era
Bombers disguised as Arab workmen and hotel waiters planted the bomb in the basement

w: At the foot of the Mount of Olives, small olive groves - divided today among several churches - are all identified with the garden where, according to the Gospels, Jesus prayed in anguish the night before his arrest. It remains one of the most resonant pilgrimage stops in Christianity, gnarled trees and all.
s: Ancient olive groves where the Gospels place Jesus's arrest
_facts: Garden and courtyard at the foot of the Mount of Olives
According to the Gospels, site of Jesus's Agony in the Garden and arrest before the crucifixion
Several small olive groves on adjoining church properties are all identified with the biblical Gethsemane

w: The Hebrew Bible first used 'Mount Zion' for the City of David, then shifted it to the Temple Mount, and only later did it settle on this hill outside the Old City's southern wall - the Western Hill of ancient Jerusalem. In its widest sense the same word, Zion, has come to stand for the entire Land of Israel.
s: A name that has meant three hills, and a whole land
_facts: Hill just outside the Old City walls to the south
Term originally applied in the Hebrew Bible to the City of David, later to the Temple Mount
Now used as the name of ancient Jerusalem's Western Hill; more broadly a name for the Land of Israel

w: This Jewish Quarter museum is run by an organization whose stated long-term goal is building a Third Temple on the Temple Mount, on the site the Dome of the Rock now occupies. It has commissioned priestly garments, ritual vessels and building plans, all made ready in case the project ever proceeds.
s: A museum stocked with garments for a temple not yet built
_facts: Organization focused on establishing a Third Temple on the Temple Mount
Runs a museum in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City
Has developed Temple ritual objects, garments and building plans
Founded and headed by Rabbi Israel Ariel

w: Near Jaffa Gate, the citadel layers Hasmonean, Herodian, Byzantine and early Muslim fortifications under a shell that is mostly Mamluk and Ottoman. The name Tower of David originally belonged to a single Herodian tower, then jumped to a 17th-century minaret before settling, since 1967, on the whole complex.
s: A citadel with five empires stacked inside it
_facts: Ancient citadel and museum near the Jaffa Gate
Current structure dates to the Mamluk and Ottoman periods, built on earlier Hasmonean, Herodian and Byzantine fortifications
Name 'Tower of David' has referred to different parts of the site over time, and since 1967 to the whole citadel

w: Parked in the government complex beside the Knesset, this library holds more than five million books and the world's largest collections of Hebraica and Judaica - alongside rare manuscripts and artifacts that make it the de facto keeper of Jewish written heritage worldwide.
s: The world's biggest trove of Hebraica, beside the Knesset
_facts: Holds more than 5 million books
Owns the world's largest collections of Hebraica and Judaica
Located in the government complex near the Knesset

w: One of only seven working gates through the Old City's walls, known equally as St Stephen's Gate, and the direct route into the Muslim Quarter. Simple, functional stonework, still doing exactly the job it was built for, gate after gate, century after century of pilgrims and traders passing through.
s: One of seven gates guarding the Old City's walls
_facts: One of the seven open gates of the Old City of Jerusalem
Also known as St Stephen's Gate
Leads into the Muslim Quarter

w: Named for Theodor Herzl, founder of modern Zionism, whose tomb crowns the summit, this hill on the western edge of the city doubles as Israel's national cemetery and resting place for its war dead. Yad Vashem, the Holocaust memorial, sits just to the west.
s: Zionism's founder, buried atop his namesake hill
_facts: Named after Theodor Herzl, founder of modern Zionism
Site of Israel's national cemetery and Herzl's tomb
Yad Vashem lies just to the west of the hill
